text.text: Your dental office in one place. Start with Appointments for today's schedule, then check recalls under Patients, plans waiting for a decision, and claims that need a follow-up call. Operational tracking only; clinical charting lives in your clinical system.
From the first phone call to the end of the first visit. A new patient who leaves without a next appointment is the most expensive mistake a dental office makes.
Ask how they heard about you and what brought them in: pain, a cleaning, a second opinion, or cosmetic work. Pain gets an emergency slot within 24 hours.
Add them under Patients with status
. Record phone, email, insurance carrier and the member ID from their card.
Offer two specific times, not "when works for you". New patient exams need 90 minutes in an operatory with the panoramic machine free.
Send the registration and health history forms by email the same day. Ask them to bring photo ID and the insurance card.
Benefits verified with the carrier: frequency limits on cleanings and X-rays, deductible met so far, annual maximum remaining, waiting periods on major work.
date filled in on the patient row.
Prior X-rays requested from the previous dentist if taken in the last 12 months (saves the patient a duplicate exposure and saves a denied claim).
Forms returned. If not, a reminder call.
Greet by name, scan the ID and card, confirm the address and phone.
Review the health history with the patient, especially blood thinners, heart conditions that need premedication, and allergies to anesthetic or latex. The clinical team reads it before seating.
Exam, full-mouth X-rays and periodontal charting happen in the chair. The dentist presents findings at the end of the visit.
The dentist's findings become rows under
, one per phase, with a fee and your insurance estimate. See Presenting a treatment plan.

Hygiene recall is the heartbeat of a practice: most restorative work is found at a cleaning. This page is how the front desk keeps every active patient on a schedule and brings back the ones who drifted.
When a cleaning is completed, set Next recall to the visit date plus the interval and book it before the patient leaves. Pre-booked recalls are kept far more often than ones scheduled by phone later.
The Patients list has three views that matter:
Open Patients, Overdue view. Sort by Next recall, oldest first.
For each patient with no future appointment, call once, text once, then email. Write the outcome in the row's page so the next person does not repeat it.
Patients who book: set the appointment and leave status Active.
Patients who say no or do not answer after three attempts over a month: status
stays, and they go on the quarterly letter list.
Patients overdue more than 18 months: move to
. Do not delete them; they come back, and their history matters.
"Hi Marisol, it's Bea from Larkspur Dental. You're due for your cleaning and Dr. Raman has Tuesday at 8 or Thursday at 4 open. Would either of those work?"

before the call so you know whether anything else is waiting.

text.text: Diagnosed treatment that never gets scheduled is the largest hidden number in most offices. This is how to present plans so patients understand them, and how to follow up so they do not quietly disappear.
The dentist enters each finding as a row under
: what it is, the teeth involved, priority and fee.
from the verified benefits: percentage covered for that category (preventive, basic, major), deductible still owed and annual maximum left.
column works out what the patient pays. Round nothing; patients remember the number you said.
The conversation (in a quiet room, not at the counter)
Start with why: "The crack on the back tooth will keep spreading, and a crown now avoids a root canal later."
Show the X-ray or intraoral photo the dentist used.
Give the total, the insurance estimate and their share, in that order. Say plainly that it is an estimate until the carrier pays.
Offer phasing when the total is large. Urgent work in this benefit year, the rest after the maximum renews.
Offer the payment options the office actually has. Never invent a discount on the spot.

and set a reminder seven days out on the plan's page.
and write the reason (cost, fear, wants a second opinion). Declined plans are reviewed at month end; reasons tell you what to change.

text.text: For crowns, bridges, implants and periodontal work over a few hundred dollars, send a pre-treatment estimate to the carrier first (a
claim row works for tracking it). Tell the patient when you expect the answer, usually two to four weeks.
Every finding from the exam has a plan row
Insurance estimate filled in before presenting
Accepted plans have an appointment on the calendar
Most denied claims are preventable at the front desk. Verify before the visit, attach what the carrier asks for, and chase every unpaid claim on a schedule.
For each patient on the next two days of the schedule whose
date is more than 30 days old:
Check eligibility on the carrier's portal or by phone.
Note frequency limits (cleanings twice a year, bitewings once a year, full-mouth X-rays every three to five years).
Note deductible remaining, annual maximum remaining and any waiting period on major services.
Update the date on the patient row.
When a visit is completed, add a row under
with the procedure codes, amount and payer, linked to the patient and the treatment plan.
Attach what the codes need: X-rays and a short narrative for crowns, perio charting for scaling and root planing, a pre-op photo for build-ups.
Send it the same day and press
for 14 days later (30 days for paper claims).
view. These are claims past their follow-up date and still not paid.
Call or check the portal for each one. Ask: received? processed? what is missing?
Write what you learned on the claim's page and set a new follow-up date. Do not leave a claim with a date in the past.
Fix and resend when the reason is clerical (wrong member ID, missing tooth number, missing X-ray), then mark it
If the service is not covered, bill the patient their portion and explain it the same week, not three months later.

A working home for the business side of a dental office: who is in the chair today, who is overdue for a cleaning, which treatment is waiting on a yes, and which insurance money has not arrived. Clinical notes and X-rays stay in your charting software; this is where the front desk and the office manager run the day.
: every booked visit with the operatory, provider and chair time. The Today view is the morning huddle; Calendar is the week at a glance.

: one row per patient with insurance, the date benefits were last checked, recall interval and next recall date. The money columns show what insurance still owes and how much treatment is diagnosed but not yet booked.
: what the dentist diagnosed, the fee, your insurance estimate and the patient's share. A plan moves from Proposed to Accepted to Scheduled to Completed, or ends Declined.
: one row per claim sent to a carrier, with procedure codes, follow-up date and denial reason.
: what is on the shelf, when to reorder, and anything that expires.

text.text: on appointments stamp the status and date for you.
on treatment plans record when the patient said yes and when the work was done.
on claims keep the insurance list honest.
One person owns each day's schedule; their name sits in Front desk owner.
Never leave a completed visit without a next appointment or a recall date.
Write the denial reason on every denied claim; the patterns tell you which narratives and X-rays carriers want.
